Imprint: Memory Without Curation - Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies

Posted to arXiv on 9 October 2026 · arXiv 2610.14406 ↗

Keep every stream, compress it as you go, and learn what to remember.

October 22, 20267 min read

robot-memoryvla

I've been interested in memory systems for a while, so I looked for one I could port to LeRobot, which I love, and I picked this one. It's an interesting system because the memory is a set of vectors that's more expressive than text, and I feel like that's where memory for robots is going. As I said in my post on robot memory, I think memory is a big bottleneck for long-horizon tasks. Reproducing Imprint taught me a lot. I found a couple of bugs and opened pull requests #10 and #11 to fix them, and the release is missing the recorded scenes the RoboCasa evaluation replays, so I emailed the authors to ask for them. In this short article I just want to share what the method is about and why I find it so interesting. In the Cover Blocks task, red, green and blue blocks sit in a random order. The robot covers them with three lids, then must uncover them in red, green, blue order. Once they're covered, every order looks the same, so how does the policy know which to open first? It has to remember. Most memory methods pick what to keep, but Imprint compresses the video, actions and joint states into a fixed set of 256 memory tokens, updated as the episode runs. With Imprint, π0.5 goes from 25.4% to 72.8% success on RMBench's nine memory tasks, the best among memory methods compared.

Stage 1 needs no policy and no human labels, since the recording itself is the target. What gets rebuilt, and at what rate?+

Is the visual target pixels, or a frame embedding?

Not pixels. The target zkvz^v_kzkv​ is a frame embedding from DINOv3 ViT-B/16, a frozen pretrained image model. Imprint averages each camera's 16 × 16 patch grid to 8 × 8, giving 64 patches of 768 numbers, so 192 × 768 per step across three cameras. Each predicted and target patch vector gets a LayerNorm with no learned scale or shift, then mean squared error with weight λv=1\lambda_v = 1λv​=1. The memory also reads these features for its newest frames, up to three not yet in a video chunk. Older frames reach it only as compressed video tokens, so the decoder has to rebuild their DINOv3 features from mtm_tmt​. It never rebuilds the tokens themselves.

How do streams at different rates line up?

No stream is resampled to another's rate, and nothing is interpolated. In RMBench, video, joint states and actions share one step index, and the memory keeps every second step of all three. Four kept steps, eight simulator steps, make a video chunk, and up to three leftover frames go in as DINOv3 tokens with their actions and joint states. Only actions that already ran go in: in training, each kept frame gets the previous kept step's action. Each training example uses one of eight stored, time-sampled frame lists, while evaluation keeps exactly every second step. The memory is written and read once per policy call, after each 50-action chunk runs.

The paper's only rate is the real robot's: each 30-action chunk runs at a nominal 30 Hz, about a second of motion. It doesn't give the simulator's rate, any camera frame rate, or whether the real robot keeps every second step, and the simulation-only public code can't fill that in.

Do they rebuild joint states, predict them, or neither?

Yes, it rebuilds them. In RMBench, joint states (the paper's proprioception) are an input stream and a Stage 1 target. The target is the raw joint vector, 14 values (arm joints and grippers) zero-padded to 16, unnormalized, and the loss averages the squared error over all 16, with weight λq=0.5\lambda_q = 0.5λq​=0.5. The decoder sees only mtm_tmt​ and a learned query naming which step to rebuild. Training picks up to 16 random kept steps, all at or before now, so the decoder rebuilds the past and forecasts nothing. Forecasting is the policy's job: RMBench actions are absolute joint positions, so each action chunk forecasts joint targets. Stage 2 drops the decoder.
